summary: Life on Mars is a free browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. You play a junior astronaut running a small Mars outpost for 7 sols (Mars days). Four bars (Power, Air, Food and Shield) start at 75. Every action helps one bar but costs another, so kids see the result of each choice straight away. The game warns you the evening before a solar flare and a dust storm. After each event, a short science note shows its source link. It answers the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning mission planning, limited resources and space weather into a living simulation instead of a quiz. It matters because kids learn to plan, make trade-offs and understand why astronauts need protection, just by playing, with nothing to install.
details:
The player walks around a 3D Mars outpost, goes to a station and presses E. Each of the four stations changes the bars: Solar panels, Air recycler, Greenhouse and Shield wall. Each sol has one action, then a night that drains every bar. A “tomorrow” number under each bar shows the cost ahead. A solar flare hits on Sol 3 and a dust storm on Sol 5, and both are warned the evening before. The player loses if any bar reaches 0 and wins by surviving 7 nights. Stars are given for how few bars ended in the red. The game also has a rover you can drive, four places to explore, small missions and a phone screen.

Benefits. Kids practise planning ahead, weighing trade-offs and reading simple numbers. There is no reading-heavy text, and it runs in a normal desktop browser.

Intended impact. We want kids to feel that being an astronaut is about careful choices and teamwork with real science, and to get curious about space weather.

Tools and languages. HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one file, with no build tools. Three.js (3D graphics) and the browser’s Pointer Lock feature for mouse look. All art is made in code: no image, audio, video or 3D model files. Developed on one laptop. Hosted on GitHub Pages. Code was written with AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic).

Creativity. A simulation where every choice has a visible cost, an astronaut you can steer and a rover you can drive, a story intro, places to explore, and a dancing astronaut when you win.

Factors we considered. Kid-friendly text sizes (at least 20px) and colors, about 60 fps on school laptops, no people under 18 shown, and no NASA logos. We kept the science honest: we use only facts we can link to and mark the made-up story as made-up.
